extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of ancient philosophy / general readers of Plato's Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Examination and critique of competing definitions of justice through Socratic dialogue (Book I of Plato's Republic), weighing proposed accounts and testing them with counterexamples and analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice = speaking the truth and paying your debts
rubrics_metrics.description: Cephalus' proposed definition: 'to speak the truth and to pay your debts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates offers counterexamples (e.g., returning weapons to a friend who is not in his right mind) to show exceptions where this formulation fails; therefore this simple formula is judged inadequate as a full definition of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice = giving to each what is proper (doing good to friends and harm to enemies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simonides' / Polemarchus' view rendered as 'the repayment of a debt' or, more plainly, that justice is 'to do good to friends and harm to enemies' — i.e., giving each what is due or proper to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained by analogy to arts (medicine gives remedies to bodies, cookery seasons food). Socrates and others probe ambiguities: who counts as friend/enemy (appearance vs reality)? If one errs about who is good or bad, the rule yields immoral outcomes. Ultimately Socrates argues that injuring a person makes them worse in the virtue proper to humans, and since the good cannot make others bad, this account is rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is useful when things are kept and useless when they are used
rubrics_metrics.description: Polemarchus' inference that justice is primarily useful for preserving or keeping things safe (e.g., keeping deposits), but is not the skill needed when those things are to be used (e.g., using a shield or lyre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: justice is useful for keeping a pruning-hook or a shield safe, but for using them better arts (vine-dresser, soldier) are required. Socrates draws out the implication that on this account justice is not broadly useful, prompting further critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice = the interest of the stronger
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrasymachus' bold definition: 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He argues that governments (tyranny, aristocracy, democracy) make laws to serve their own interests, and those laws define justice for their subjects. Socrates challenges this by pointing out rulers can be mistaken and by questioning what 'stronger' or 'interest' precisely mean. Thrasymachus refines by insisting on a strict sense of 'ruler' (an expert, unerring ruler), but the dialogue probes internal inconsistencies and consequences of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: A just person cannot harm another; virtue cannot produce vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Socratic argument that to injure someone is to make them worse in the proper virtue of humans (justice), and the good (virtue) cannot make anyone bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses analogies (a musician cannot by his art make people unmusical; heat does not produce cold) to conclude that justice cannot consist in harming others. This principle is used to reject accounts of justice that require injuring people (e.g., harming enemies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must be clear and accurate; avoid equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrasymachus' demand for 'clearness and accuracy' and Socrates' emphasis on precise meanings in philosophical inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dialogue repeatedly tests proposed definitions by seeking precise senses of key terms (e.g., 'interest', 'stronger', 'friend'). Socratic method (questioning, counterexamples, analogy) is used as the procedural standard for evaluating definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'interest' of an art is the perfection of its subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates' claim that every art's interest consists in the perfection or proper good of its subject (medicine aims at health, pilot at safe navigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is used to interrogate Thrasymachus' claim: if the interest of a ruler/office is the perfection of its subject (the city's good), then 'interest' should not be equated merely with rulers' material advantage. The point reframes 'interest' as the flourishing/perfection of the thing governed rather than raw advantage to a ruler.
